paragraphs: The paper investigates how an arm movement changes when a target moves twice in quick succession. With intervals of 10–110 milliseconds between the target presentations, the hand initially travels toward a position between the two targets. The behavior therefore calls for an explanation of how successive target information combines during movement.

The proposed explanation adds two independent movement components as vectors. One component moves the hand toward an internally specified location. The other moves it from that internal location toward the final target. Adding these components accounts for the observed movement characteristics, connecting the curved or redirected trajectory to simpler point-to-point motions.

The inferred internal locations also resemble endpoints previously measured for the first rapid eye movements in comparable target-displacement studies. That resemblance suggests a possible connection between how hand and eye control represent target location. The paper presents this as a suggestion, while its central computational result is that superimposed movement components explain the modified hand trajectories.
neurips-1991-a-computational-mechanism-t.tldr: Adding two independent movement components explains hand trajectories that initially head between rapidly changing targets.

paragraphs: This paper addresses classification problems where examples from different classes lie very close together. In these narrow regions, a useful decision boundary must separate nearby points while following potentially complicated shapes. The proposed network builds that boundary from locally trained flat segments, allowing different regions to receive their own separating rules.

Its basic component combines a local linear discriminator with Gaussian functions describing how nearby training data are distributed relative to the separating plane. This combination makes the component sensitive to both separation and locality. A modified perceptron learning procedure finds the separators, and a constructive algorithm adds components to the hidden layer for two-class problems.

The output combines these local decisions into a smooth boundary assembled from linear pieces. Preliminary results show successful separation in cases where standard multilayer perceptrons and nearest-neighbor classification have high training error. The stated finding concerns fitting difficult boundaries in the training data; its significance is that local geometric structure can make closely spaced classes easier to separate.
neurips-1991-a-network-of-localized-line.tldr: A network of local separators learns complex, narrow class boundaries by combining simple decisions fitted to nearby data.

paragraphs: The paper describes a fabricated signal-processing chip for vector–matrix multiplication. This operation combines the entries of an input vector according to values stored in a matrix. The chip performs the computation in parallel, making the physical organization of the hardware central to how the arithmetic is carried out.

The matrix is represented by analog electrical charge held in an array of charge-coupled devices. Each stored charge encodes a matrix element. Input vectors, by contrast, are digital and support accuracy from one to eight bits. The design therefore combines analog storage of the matrix with a digital representation of the incoming values.

The device uses a two-micrometer CCD/CMOS fabrication process and implements single-quadrant multiplication, which restricts the supported operand signs. Its contribution is a concrete hardware realization of this parallel computation with two different numerical representations. The reported design connects the matrix directly to a charge-storage array, while allowing the digital input representation to use different levels of precision.
neurips-1991-a-parallel-analog-ccd-cmos-.tldr: A fabricated CCD/CMOS chip performs parallel vector–matrix multiplication using analog matrix storage and digital inputs.

paragraphs: The paper explains why encouraging a neural network to keep its weights small can improve predictions on new examples. It begins with linear networks, where the effects of weight decay can be analyzed directly. The analysis separates two benefits that help explain previously observed improvements in numerical experiments.

First, weight decay removes irrelevant components of the weight vector by selecting the smallest vector that solves the learning problem. This means the solution avoids weight components that do not help satisfy the task. Second, a suitably chosen amount of decay reduces some effects of fixed noise in the training targets, improving generalization.

The strength of decay matters to the noise-related benefit: the claim depends on choosing its size appropriately. The paper then extends the results to networks containing hidden layers and nonlinear units, and reports numerical confirmation using NetTalk data. Together, the analysis and simulations explain weight decay through both the removal of unnecessary weight components and reduced sensitivity to noisy target values.
neurips-1991-a-simple-weight-decay-can-i.tldr: Weight decay can improve generalization by removing irrelevant weight components and reducing the influence of noisy targets.

paragraphs: Comparing neural-network training methods can depend heavily on how long each run is allowed to continue. This paper identifies the training epoch limit as a problem for existing performance measures: choosing a different stopping limit can change the result of a comparison. It proposes measures intended to avoid that arbitrary dependence.

The central efficiency measure relates the number of successfully trained networks to the training effort spent obtaining them. This frames learning performance as a balance between successful outcomes and computational effort. Within that framework, the optimal epoch limit is the stopping point that achieves the highest efficiency, making the limit something to determine systematically.

The paper also models learning performance statistically and estimates its asymptotic behavior, meaning its behavior as training extends further. These ideas connect practical decisions about when to stop training with a broader account of learning success. The contribution is a framework for comparing training performance and choosing useful stopping limits, rather than treating a manually selected training budget as an unquestioned benchmark.
neurips-1991-benchmarking-feed-forward-n.tldr: New benchmarking measures compare successful training against effort and identify an efficiency-maximizing training limit.

paragraphs: The paper presents NNC2, a charge-coupled-device processor implementing a fully connected network with 192 inputs and 32 outputs. Its two-layer organization provides a hardware building block for neural computation. Multiple devices can be cascaded to create more layers or operated in parallel to increase the number of input or output nodes.

The processor stores programmable network weights in digital memory on the chip, with six-bit weight accuracy. At a clock rate of 10 MHz, it computes 1.92 billion connections per second. These specifications describe both the numerical precision of the stored connections and the rate at which the device processes them.

The authors also describe a pattern-recognition system combining NNC2 with CCD image feature extractors. A separate output circuit uses nonlinear behavior in charge injection to implement a sigmoid with an adjustable threshold in an area of 40 by 80 square micrometers. Together, the components address feature extraction, weighted network computation, and nonlinear output processing within a CCD-based hardware approach.
neurips-1991-ccd-neural-network-processo.tldr: The NNC2 processor combines programmable neural-network hardware with CCD feature extraction and a compact sigmoid circuit.

paragraphs: Radial basis function networks classify examples using their distances from a collection of centers. In the version considered here, those centers are initially selected without using the desired outputs. The paper asks which parts of this distance-based representation benefit most from supervised learning, testing three modifications on the NETtalk task.

Learning a non-Euclidean distance measure reduces the network's error rate, indicating that the ordinary geometric distance is not always the most useful measure for classification. Learning each center's variance produces inferior performance. The strongest improvement comes from generalized radial basis function networks, which use supervised learning to determine the center locations themselves.

After training on 1,000 words, the standard RBF network correctly classifies 56.5% of letters in a separate test set, while the generalized version reaches 73.4%. These results support the paper's conclusion that center placement can be especially important. Using the desired outputs to decide where centers belong changes the reference points underlying the network's predictions and substantially improves accuracy in this experiment.
neurips-1991-improving-the-performance-o.tldr: Supervised learning of RBF center locations substantially improves test accuracy on NETtalk.

paragraphs: This paper develops a nonlinear regression method that builds a polynomial gradually. A sparse polynomial uses a selected collection of terms, allowing the fitted relationship to include nonlinear effects without requiring every possible term. Construction proceeds from lower-order terms toward higher-order terms, so the approximation grows in complexity through successive decisions.

The key selection mechanism looks ahead to predict whether an input variable can help explain the error that remains. This guides the addition of new terms. The algorithm extends a tree-growing heuristic from LMS Trees to approximate arbitrary polynomials of the input features, and the paper supplies a new theoretical justification for that heuristic.

Two demonstrations illustrate what this construction can achieve. The algorithm recovers a known polynomial from sampled observations and accurately estimates pixel values in an image-processing task. The first result shows recovery of an underlying mathematical relationship; the second shows usefulness for estimating image data. Together, they support selective polynomial growth as a practical approach to nonlinear approximation.
neurips-1991-iterative-construction-of-s.tldr: A look-ahead algorithm builds sparse polynomials by selecting terms that can explain the remaining prediction error.

paragraphs: JANUS is a system for translating spoken language into speech in another language. It accepts continuous speech in English and German and produces translations in German, English, and Japanese. The paper presents the complete system, making the interaction among its processing components part of the research contribution.

The system combines connectionist learning with traditional artificial-intelligence knowledge representations, dynamic programming, and statistical techniques. These approaches provide different ways to learn patterns, represent knowledge, organize computations, and handle uncertainty. JANUS uses them within one translation system, and its interchangeable components allow alternative processing choices to be evaluated within that shared setting.

The reported translation fidelity is 87% for English speech input and 97% for German speech input. These figures describe translation performance according to the paper's fidelity measure. The authors also present comparative evaluations of individual processing components, emphasizing the connectionist modules. The work therefore connects overall translation results with an examination of how different computational approaches contribute inside a working speech-to-speech system.
neurips-1991-janus-speech-to-speech-tran.tldr: JANUS combines neural and other AI methods for speech-to-speech translation, reporting 87% fidelity from English and 97% from German.

paragraphs: The paper studies a proposed way to improve neural-network generalization: create artificial training examples by adding noise to the original training vectors. A feed-forward network then learns using backpropagation with these perturbed examples. The central question is how this training procedure relates to established statistical methods for estimating relationships from data.

The authors connect noisy backpropagation training to kernel density estimation and kernel regression. These connections provide a statistical perspective on what happens when training data are spread into nearby variations. The focus is therefore both a practical training modification and an interpretation of that modification through another family of estimation methods.

Simulated examples compare ordinary backpropagation, backpropagation with added noise, and kernel regression. The comparisons cover both mapping estimation, where the task is to predict a relationship, and pattern classification, where the task is to assign categories. The stated contribution is the connection and comparative investigation across these settings; the abstract does not identify one method as the overall winner.
neurips-1991-kernel-regression-and-backp.tldr: The paper connects noise-augmented backpropagation to kernel estimation and compares the methods on prediction and classification tasks.

paragraphs: Inverse kinematics asks which robot configuration produces a desired position in its workspace. The difficulty addressed here is that the forward mapping from configuration to workspace need not have a unique inverse. The paper develops a bootstrap method that learns an inverse using only sampled pairs of configurations and workspace locations.

The method first uses unsupervised clustering on neighborhoods of configurations associated with workspace points. Its purpose is to partition configuration space into subsets where the forward mapping is invertible. Supervised learning then fits a separate inverse function within each subset, giving each learner a relationship with a well-defined direction back to configurations.

This combination turns an ill-posed inverse problem into a collection of better-defined learning problems. The authors demonstrate a global inverse-kinematics solution for a wristless Puma manipulator. The contribution lies in learning the partition as well as the inverse mappings: the organization of the data resolves ambiguity before supervised approximation is applied to the individual regions.
neurips-1991-learning-global-direct-inve.tldr: Clustering separates robot configurations into invertible regions so supervised learners can build a global inverse-kinematics solution.

paragraphs: MAGIC learns how to group image features according to the objects they belong to. This matters when several objects overlap, because recognition requires deciding which features go together. The system learns from examples whose segmentation is already provided, allowing the grouping rules themselves to be acquired through training.

Grouping takes place in a relaxation network whose features exchange complex-valued signals. Each signal has an amplitude and a phase, and related features become bound together by locking their phases. This supplies a changing representation of group membership within the network. Training extends recurrent backpropagation to units that operate with these complex-valued signals.

The paper reports that MAGIC often discovers grouping rules resembling previously proposed heuristics, while also being capable of finding less intuitive structural regularities. That result connects familiar image-grouping principles with a mechanism that can learn additional ones from examples. The approach makes segmentation a learned interaction among features, addressing the feature-assignment problem that otherwise complicates recognition in scenes with multiple objects.
neurips-1991-learning-to-segment-images-.tldr: MAGIC learns image segmentation by synchronizing the phases of related features in a complex-valued recurrent network.

paragraphs: The paper improves a family of parallel analog methods for finding approximate solutions to difficult combinatorial problems. These methods use mean-field approximations derived from statistical mechanics and normally require an externally chosen annealing schedule. That schedule controls how the optimization process changes as it progresses toward a solution.

The proposed approach combines a given mean-field algorithm with ideas from constrained optimization and adaptive simulated annealing. The combination produces a unified parallel relaxation procedure that no longer needs an externally prescribed schedule. This integrates the management of the annealing process into the optimization method itself, addressing a practical requirement of the earlier algorithms.

Numerical simulations on traveling-salesman problems with 50 and 100 cities show that the combined algorithms are typically about ten times faster than the mean-field algorithms alone. They also sometimes produce better solutions. The findings concern approximate optimization: the main reported advantage is a large speed improvement, accompanied in some cases by an improvement in solution quality.
neurips-1991-merging-constrained-optimis.tldr: Combining constrained optimization with adaptive annealing removes an external schedule and typically speeds tested TSP solvers by about tenfold.

paragraphs: This paper considers how computational models might explain the linked changes in brain activity and mental experience across waking and sleep. Its starting point is that these state changes have a specific organization. A model must therefore address relationships among states as well as neural activity within an individual state.

Existing work represents cyclic changes in brainstem cell populations using variants of Volterra–Lotka equations. The authors identify a further modeling need: neural networks that incorporate knowledge of the populations' particular connections and their differing responses to drugs. These biological details provide concrete structure that models of sleep and waking should account for.

The paper summarizes preliminary attempts to connect the neurophysiology of rapid eye movement sleep with the cognitive characteristics of dreaming through neural-network approaches. It also describes modeling across states as being at an early stage. Its contribution is an account of this modeling direction and its biological requirements, together with initial efforts to link neural mechanisms to dream cognition.
neurips-1991-models-wanted-must-fit-dime.tldr: The paper outlines biological requirements and preliminary neural-network efforts for connecting sleep physiology with dreaming.

paragraphs: The paper extends neural recognition of isolated handwritten digits to unconstrained strings containing several digits. Reading a string involves both identifying the digits and deciding how the image should be divided among them. The proposed feed-forward architecture combines a repeated digit recognizer with a module that selects an interpretation of the whole input.

A single-digit recognizer is replicated across the input, and the network's output feeds a Viterbi alignment module. That module chooses the best interpretation among possible alignments. Training errors pass back through the alignment module, so learning incorporates information from the interpretation selected for the digit string.

The distinctive feature is where segmentation happens: it operates on feature maps developed by the Space Displacement Neural Network rather than directly on image pixels. This lets the division into digits use the network's internal representation of the handwriting. The contribution is an architecture and training procedure that connect recognition, alignment, and segmentation within the same system for interpreting multiple handwritten digits.
neurips-1991-multi-digit-recognition-usi.tldr: A replicated digit recognizer and Viterbi alignment module segment handwritten digit strings using learned feature maps.

paragraphs: This paper addresses neural control when available data are insufficient but useful domain knowledge already exists. The motivating application is a hot-line rolling mill. The authors consider analytical theories that describe the application imperfectly and ask how those theories can still contribute systematically to learning an accurate control model.

Their answer uses a Bayesian framework to incorporate prior knowledge into networks of locally tuned units. The knowledge influences both the choice of network architecture and the training regimen. This makes domain theory part of how the model is constructed and learned, allowing imperfect analytical information to contribute alongside the available observations.

In the large-scale rolling-mill application, the method successfully addresses data deficiency and achieves substantially higher accuracy than optimally tuned standard algorithms, including sigmoidal backpropagation. It also outperforms the existing state-of-the-art solution. The stated result supports the value of using application knowledge to shape learning when data alone are inadequate, with the evidence coming from this industrial control setting.
neurips-1991-neural-control-for-rolling-.tldr: A Bayesian method embeds imperfect domain theory into neural architecture and training to improve rolling-mill control with limited data.

paragraphs: The paper applies neural networks to detecting avascular necrosis of the femoral head from magnetic resonance images. The condition is described as common and potentially serious, and MRI can reveal it at a very early stage. This makes the interpretation of these images a relevant target for automated classification.

The authors develop multilayer perceptron networks that make a diagnosis from a single image of the femoral head. They train the networks using conjugate-gradient optimization, which adjusts the network parameters during learning. The resulting task connects an individual medical image to a diagnostic decision through a trained neural model.

The reported accuracy is 100% on the training data and 97% on the test data. The training result shows that the networks fit the examples used for learning, while the test result shows strong performance on the separately evaluated examples. The paper's stated finding is therefore evidence that this network approach can recognize the condition in the MRI data used in the study.
neurips-1991-neural-network-diagnosis-of.tldr: Multilayer perceptrons diagnose femoral-head avascular necrosis from individual MRI images with reported test accuracy of 97%.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how a mobile robot can learn obstacle avoidance through experience. Its experiments use a simulated vehicle equipped with a simple range sensor. The aim is to produce immediate responses to sensory input that nevertheless form organized, plan-like paths through the environment.

Avoidance behavior is represented by continuous functions over the space of perceptual inputs. These functions are stored using CMAC representations and trained with a variant of the adaptive critic algorithm. As the vehicle explores, collisions supply negative reinforcement, and the learned responses change to reduce that negative feedback.

The reported trajectories are collision-free paths through the simulated environment. Their significance is that coherent local navigation emerges from sensory responses trained toward an explicit objective: avoiding collisions. The work connects reflexive control with reinforcement learning by showing how feedback from exploration can shape a set of immediate response functions into behavior that looks organized over an extended path.
neurips-1991-obstacle-avoidance-through-.tldr: A simulated vehicle learns collision-free local navigation by adapting continuous sensory responses to collision penalties.

paragraphs: The paper presents a way to guide the internal representations of simple recurrent networks. It adds hint units, which are extra output targets used during training. These targets provide supervision that helps shape what the hidden units represent, making the network's internal organization an explicit part of the learning problem.

The authors offer two complementary interpretations of the trained network. An input pattern can be viewed as an operator that changes information stored in the context units. Conversely, a context activation pattern can be viewed as a curried function: it fixes part of a computation and determines how subsequent input sequences are processed.

Simulations show that a network can learn to represent three different functions simultaneously. The authors then use canonical discriminant analysis to examine how the operator and curried-function interpretations appear in hidden-unit activity. The contribution combines a method for shaping representations with ways to analyze them, linking recurrent computation to functional descriptions of both incoming inputs and stored context.
neurips-1991-operators-and-curried-funct.tldr: Hint targets shape recurrent-network representations that can be analyzed as input-driven operators and context-dependent functions.

paragraphs: This paper models short-term memory using excitatory neurons whose activation thresholds change over time. Those threshold dynamics include fatigue and potentiation, giving the model two mechanisms with different roles. Together, they allow a mixed input to activate distinguishable memories and keep those memories active after the input disappears.

Fatigue produces oscillations in activity. When a mixed input engages several cell assemblies, the model separates their activity into oscillations staggered in time. Each assembly corresponds to a memory, so this temporal organization provides a form of segmentation: components of the mixed input remain distinguishable through the timing of their activity.

Potentiation sustains the staggered oscillations after the external input is removed. That persistence is what makes the system a model of short-term memory. The model also has limited capacity, described as resembling the familiar range of seven plus or minus two items. Its central idea is that changing neuronal thresholds can support both temporal separation of memories and their temporary retention.
neurips-1991-oscillatory-model-of-short-.tldr: Fatigue separates memories into staggered oscillations, while potentiation keeps those oscillations active after input ends.

paragraphs: The paper asks when observed frequencies can reliably approximate true probabilities for every event in a family at once. It studies distributions over binary vectors of length n. The desired guarantee is that the largest estimation error across the event family stays below a chosen tolerance with sufficiently high probability.

Polynomial uniform convergence means that this guarantee requires a sample size growing only polynomially with the vector length, inverse error tolerance, and inverse failure probability. The distribution is part of the setting, so the analysis can account for which observations it tends to produce. This makes the question sensitive to the actual sampling distribution.

The main result gives a necessary and sufficient condition using the expected VC dimension of the event family restricted to sampled points, normalized by sample size. An appropriate polynomial decay of that quantity characterizes polynomial uniform convergence. This connects a probability-estimation guarantee to the effective complexity visible in random samples, and the paper discusses applications to distribution-dependent PAC learning.
neurips-1991-polynomial-uniform-converge.tldr: A sample-dependent VC-dimension condition exactly characterizes polynomial uniform convergence under a specified distribution.

paragraphs: The paper connects recognizing an object with learning how to manipulate it. It presents two neural controller-learning schemes based on feedback-error learning and modular architecture. Both schemes use bodily sensory information, visual information, or a combination of the two to identify objects in the course of manipulation.

The first scheme trains a gating network to develop representations specific to particular objects or groups of objects. The second trains an estimation network to represent functional properties and directly estimate physical parameters. The distinction concerns what recognition supplies to control: an object-related representation in one case and estimated physical characteristics in the other.

After learning, the control networks issue motor commands appropriate for manipulating each object. This links recognition to an action requirement rather than treating identification as an isolated output. The contribution is the pair of approaches to the same control problem, showing how either object-specific or function-specific representations can connect sensory information with the motor commands needed for different manipulated objects.
neurips-1991-recognition-of-manipulated-.tldr: Two modular neural schemes recognize manipulated objects through either object-specific representations or estimated physical parameters.

paragraphs: The paper describes an analog integrated circuit that models several aspects of auditory-nerve responses, including temporal adaptation. Temporal adaptation concerns how a response changes over time. Incorporating it makes the model sensitive to the time course of neural response, a feature the paper identifies as relevant to auditory processing.

The motivation comes from two related lines of work. Auditory theorists regard adaptation as an important part of speech coding in the auditory periphery. Experiments with models of sound localization and pitch perception also suggest that it matters for practical auditory processing. These observations motivate giving adaptation an explicit role in the circuit.

The author reports designing, fabricating, and successfully testing the integrated circuit. The stated achievement is therefore a physical implementation of an auditory-nerve response model that includes adaptation. Its significance is that a biologically motivated temporal property is realized in analog hardware, providing a concrete circuit model for a response characteristic implicated in several kinds of hearing-related computation.
neurips-1991-temporal-adaptation-in-a-si.tldr: A fabricated and tested analog circuit models auditory-nerve responses, including temporal adaptation.

paragraphs: This paper relates two ways to describe a network's capacity: VC dimension and statistical lower epsilon-capacity. VC dimension concerns the richness of a classifier family, while the statistical quantity concerns capacity under random sampling. The authors establish a relationship that gives an order-level lower bound on VC dimension from the statistical capacity.

The relationship is used to explain quantitatively how generalization occurs after memorization. It also connects consistency with the capacities of the best classifier in a fixed structural family and the Bayesian classifier. These connections place memorization and generalization within a shared analysis of what a network family can represent.

The paper then turns the relationship into a method for obtaining VC-dimension lower bounds for feed-forward networks. It applies that method to two hardware-relevant cases: a two-layer network with binary weights and specified threshold restrictions, and a single binary-weight neuron with zero threshold. The contribution combines a general capacity relationship with applications to architectures whose discrete parameters matter for hardware implementation.
neurips-1991-the-vc-dimension-versus-the.tldr: A relationship between statistical capacity and VC dimension yields lower bounds for hardware-oriented binary-weight networks.

paragraphs: VISIT is a neural-network model of visual attention, the ability to concentrate processing on a selected part of the visual field. The paper studies this ability through searching for a target among distracting objects. This task provides a concrete way to investigate how selective processing supports visual behavior.

The model's behavior closely matches known psychophysical findings about visual search and attention. It also agrees with much of the physiological evidence on attention. These two kinds of correspondence matter together: one concerns observable search behavior, while the other concerns the neural processes that a biologically plausible model should reflect.

The paper emphasizes how VISIT relates to the primary visual cortex, pulvinar, superior colliculus, and posterior parietal regions. It offers a view of the functions these areas may serve in attention. The contribution is therefore both a model of target search among distractors and a proposed biological account that connects the model's operation to several parts of the visual system.
neurips-1991-visit-a-neural-model-of-cov.tldr: VISIT models attentive visual search and matches reported behavioral and physiological findings while proposing roles for visual brain regions.
